subject: pe

moments.title: East Germany dominates Montreal
moments.body: East Germany (population 17 million) wins 40 gold medals, second only to the USSR. State Plan 14.25 — declassified after reunification — reveals a systematic doping programme involving ~10,000 athletes, with steroids administered (often without consent) from age 13. Many female athletes suffered severe long-term health consequences.
moments.takeaway: An entire country systematically doped its athletes for international prestige. The medals are still in the record books.

moments.title: Ben Johnson's Seoul disqualification
moments.body: On 24 September 1988, Canadian sprinter Ben Johnson wins the 100m in 9.79s. Three days later he tests positive for stanozolol and is stripped. Carl Lewis, who finished second, was himself reportedly let off from positive tests at the US trials (revealed 2003). The race was 'the dirtiest race in history'.
moments.takeaway: Doping at the highest level of sport in 1988 was not a one-athlete problem. It was a system.

moments.title: Russian state doping revealed
moments.body: Investigations led by ARD documentary maker Hajo Seppelt expose state-sponsored doping in Russian athletics, particularly around Sochi 2014. The McLaren Report (2016) confirms FSB involvement in switching urine samples through a 'mouse hole' in the Sochi anti-doping lab. Russia is banned, partly, from subsequent Olympics.
moments.takeaway: State-sponsored doping continued from the GDR era through to 21st-century Russia. The names of the states changed; the architecture was similar.

now.title: Anti-doping today
now.body: WADA (1999) coordinates testing, sanctions and the World Anti-Doping Code. The Athlete Biological Passport tracks longitudinal biomarkers rather than just substances. New problem areas: gene doping, micro-dosing, and disputes (Sinner, Świątek 2024) over contamination thresholds.
now.open_questions: Can anti-doping keep up with new performance technologies? The lab-cheat gap is roughly constant.

reflection: Lance Armstrong won seven Tour de France titles, then admitted (Oprah, 2013) to systematic doping. His foundation (Livestrong) raised hundreds of millions for cancer charities. Cheating and good cause can coexist in the same career.
